title: Robust subspace designs and the power of a unique small quantum witness
authors: Simon Apers, Roman Edenhofer, Benjamin Mathieu-Bloise, Partha Mukhopadhyay
abstract: The concept of subspace designs was introduced by Guruswami and Xing (STOC'13), and explicit constructions were given by Guruswami and Kopparty (FOCS'13). These are families of subspaces that have small intersection with any given subspace of a fixed dimension. We introduce \emph{robust subspace designs}. Informally, these are a quantitative extension in which we demand that not too many subspaces of the family contain directions that lie close to any given subspace of a fixed dimension. We give a probabilistic construction of such a robust subspace design of polynomial size, as well as a non-trivial explicit construction of superpolynomial size.   Our main application of this new concept is a quantum space-bounded variant of the Valiant-Vazirani theorem (Theor.Comput.Sci.'86), which shows that restricting $\mathsf{NP}$-complete problems to instances with at most one accepting witness preserves hardness under randomized reductions. For quantum witnesses, the analogous quantity is the dimension of an accepting witness subspace. We use our probabilistic construction of robust subspace designs to isolate a unique witness for space-bounded quantum Merlin-Arthur protocols with perfect completeness and an acceptance gap outside their perfectly accepting subspace.   As further applications, we give a randomized reduction of well-conditioned nullity testing to space-bounded quantum Merlin-Arthur protocols with perfect completeness. Using a similar idea, we find that ordinary subspace designs allow us to recover the classical $\mathsf{C_= L}$ containment of Allender, Beals, and Ogihara (STOC'96) for general nullity testing through a simpler proof.
summary: This paper develops the mathematical concept of 'robust subspace designs' to quantify how well a family of subspaces avoids intersecting any given subspace. It applies this theory to quantum complexity theory, proving a quantum analogue of the Valiant-Vazirani theorem by showing that restricting quantum witnesses to a unique subspace preserves computational hardness.
main_problem: The paper introduces and analyzes 'robust subspace designs' as a quantitative tool to establish quantum complexity containments.
main_result: It proves a quantum space-bounded variant of the Valiant-Vazirani theorem, specifically $	ext{FewQUMAL1} \subseteq 	ext{RLUQUMAL1}$, using these designs to isolate unique quantum witnesses.
method: The core method involves using robust subspace designs, derived via probabilistic or explicit constructions, to iteratively reduce the kernel dimension of a matrix associated with a quantum protocol.
model_or_system: The work analyzes quantum Merlin-Arthur protocols ($	ext{FewQUMAL1}$), which involve quantum witnesses, and relates them to algebraic structures like subspaces and singular values.
key_observables: The minimum non-zero eigenvalue ($\lambda_{\min}(H_x)$) of a constructed Hamiltonian $H_x$, and the dimension of the accepting witness subspace.
important_parameters: The robustness parameter ($\eta$), the acceptance gap, and the time horizon $T$ used in the Hamiltonian construction.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the existence of a 'rejection gap' ($\gamma$) and the assumption of perfect completeness for the quantum protocols analyzed.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the difference between a 'Robust' and 'Non-robust' family of planes in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
paper_structure: The paper first develops the theory of robust subspace designs (probabilistic and explicit constructions). It then applies this theory to establish the quantum complexity containment $	ext{FewQUMAL1} \subseteq 	ext{RLUQUMAL1}$ via kernel peeling, followed by related completeness proofs.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical tools developed (robust subspace designs) provide powerful techniques for analyzing the structure and hardness of quantum computational models, which is central to quantum information theory.
